title: Microscopy and the Structure of the Cell
lead: Microscopy & Structures of the Cell People contemplated the existence of microbes long ago, but the field of microbiology emerged only after microbes were visualized. Microscopes have always been an important tool for microbiologists. In this chapter, we will examine how some modern microscopes work and then discuss the structure of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

blocks.text: Microbes, by definition, are too small to be seen by the unaided eye. How small are microbes? To answer this question, we must review the units of measurement. Scientists use the International System of Units (SI) for measurement. The system employs the decimal (or metric) system. In this system, the units of length, mass, and volume are the meter (m), the gram (g), and the liter (l), respectively.

A meter is about 1.09 yards, a gram is about 0.035 ounces, and a liter is about 1.06 quarts. A tenth, a hundredth, a thousandth, a millionth, and a billionth of the above metric units are expressed by adding the prefixes deci-, centi-, mili-, micro-, and nano-, respectively, before the respective units (Table 2.1). The smaller units are more suitable for microbiology.
Table 2.1. Units of measurements.
Length 	Mass (weight) 	Volume

1 meter (m)= 1,000 millimeter (mm) 1 gram (g) =1,000 milligrams (mg) 1 liter (l)= 1,000 milliliter (ml) 1 mm=1x10-3 m =1,000 micrometers (μm) 1 mg= 1x10-3 g =1,000 micrograms (μg) 1 ml= 1x10-3 l =1,000 micro liter (μl) 1 μm=1x10-6 m =1,000 nanometers (nm) 1 μg= 1x10-6 g =1,000 nanograms (ng) 1 μl= 1x10-6 l =1,000 nanoliters (nl) 1 nm= 1x10-9 m =1000 picometers (pm) 1 ng= 1x10-9 g =1,000 picograms (pg) 1 nl= 1x10-9 l =1,000 picoliters (pl) Note: Some other frequently used metric units are centimeter (cm), angstrom (A°), kilogram (kg), and deciliter (dl). One cm= 1x10-2 m = 10 mm, one A°= 10-10 m= 0.10 nm, 1 kg= 1,000 g, and one dl= 1x10-2 l =100 ml. To put it in perspective, a typical bacterium is about 3.0 micrometers in length. The weight of such a bacterium is about 1.0 picogram or 1x10-12 gram, and the bacterial cell contains about 0.002 picoliters or 2x10-15 liters of cytoplasm.

A light microscope (LM) uses visible or ultraviolet light to generate an image of a microbe. A modern LM is a compound microscope because it contains two or more sets of lenses. A light beam is channeled through a diaphragm, and a set of condenser lenses concentrates the light into a cone shape, focusing the beam on the specimen mounted on a glass slide. The beam emerging from the specimen passes through one (or a set of) objective lenses, and finally one (or a set of) ocular lenses (Fig. 2.1). A magnified image is initially generated by the objective lens, and the ocular lens magnifies the image again. The eye or a camera sees a virtual image of the object on a bright background. A compound microscope is thus a bright-field microscope.

The glass lenses used in light microscopes have a low (about 200 nm) resolving power (Fig. 2.2). An image is considered resolved if two closely positioned objects can be plainly distinguished as two objects. A microscope with a resolving power of 200 means it can resolve two objects placed 200 nm apart. The plasma membrane of a cell could not be viewed at this level of resolution. The recently developed stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy has achieved a resolution of 50 nm using glass lenses and fluorescent staining technology.
Fig. 2.1. A compound microscope and its major limitations. A. How a light microscope creates an image of a

specimen. The optical image of a tiny specimen is shown as a green arrow, and the virtual image of the same specimen is shown as a red arrow. Optics is drawn after images of an incident light microscope, Olympus America, Waltham, MA. B. Differences between poor resolution and high resolution, and low contrast and high contrast. Image courtesy: Wikipedia. C. A diagram showing why oil immersion is necessary for generating a sharper image. A light ray passing from glass to oil (shown in blue) would enter the objective lens; a ray passing from glass to air (shown in red) may disperse away.

Two other problems with resolution are the contrast (differentiation) and refraction of light (Fig. 2.1). The cell and its organelles are generally transparent. Since the glass lens is also transparent, light microscopes require contrast enhancement, which is typically achieved by staining the sample or using special optics (see Section 2.3). Staining, however, may kill or deform microbial specimens.

Light passing from one medium (say, air) to another (say, water) bends if they have different refractive indices (Fig. 2.1). Thus, some light rays emerging from the specimen do not enter the optical lens, making the image poorly resolved, especially if a high-power lens is used. This issue can be solved by immersing the specimen in immersion oil with a refractive index matching that of air (Fig. 2.1).
Power and magnification of lenses

The power of a lens (the extent to which a lens can converge or diverge a light beam) is the inverse of its focal length (i.e., 1/f, where f is the focal length), whereas the magnification (M) of the same is the ratio of the height of the image (h’) to the height of the original object (h) (i.e., M=h’/h, see Fig. 2.2). The focal length is the distance between the center of the lens and the point where the light beam converges.
Fig. 2.2. Power and magnifying ability of a biconvex lens. The focal length, the object's height, and the image's
height are indicated. Redrawn after Teacho.com.

The magnifying ability of a lens is expressed as a multiple (x). The condenser lens does not magnify. Compound LMs generally use four objective lenses with powers of 4x, 10x, 50x, and 100x, and one ocular lens with a 10x magnification. The total magnification achieved by an LM is the multiple of the magnifying power of the objective lens and that of the ocular lens. Thus, the total magnification of an object is 1,000x if a 100x objective and a 10x ocular lens were used. If a bacterium is 2 micrometers in length, its image would appear 2x1,000= 2,000 micrometers or 2 mm if a 100x objective and a 10x ocular lens were used to examine it. You will learn more details on the optics of light microscopes in a laboratory course associated with this course.

blocks.text: Some of the commonly used contrast-enhancing LMs are briefly described here. These microscopes can be used to view unstained live specimens.
Dark-field microscopes

The condenser of a dark-field microscope contains an opaque disc that prevents light from passing through the unstained specimen but allows scattered light to enter the specimen (Fig. 2.3). Light emerging from the specimen bends (refracts and reflects) again before entering the objective lens. The image appears glassy, with a visible edge, on a dark background (Fig. 2.3). Live organisms, including spermatozoa and motile protozoa, can be observed under a dark-field microscope.
Fig. 2.3. Contrast-enhancing microscopes. The common (indicated by numbers) and special components (as

labeled) of a typical dark-field, phase-contrast, and DIC microscope. The light paths are indicated. Images of a live amoeba (a protozoan) generated by each of the microscopes are shown below. Note that a dark field image only shows the margin of the specimen, and a phase-contrast image is more enhanced, but a DIC microscope produces almost a 3-D image with some internal details of the live specimen. 1- light source, 2- condenser lens, 3- specimen on a glass slide, 4- objective lens, 5- ocular lens. The three images of an amoeba are from http://www.microscopy-uk.org.uk/. Phase-contrast microscopes The condenser of a phase-contrast microscope contains an annular diaphragm that allows direct light as well as scattered light to pass through the unstained live specimen. Biological specimens have denser and less dense areas, and those areas absorb and diffract light at different degrees, causing a phase change (a change in the angle of the light beam) of the outgoing light. The diffraction plate of the microscope converts the phase change of the light rays into an amplitude (oscillation of light waves) change (Fig. 2.3). The images of the different parts of the specimen display different degrees of brightness. Phase-contrast images may show a halo effect (bright or dark ring) at their margins.

Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopes DIC microscopes are modified phase-contrast microscopes that use polarized light sources. Polarized light waves vibrate only in one plane (the waves of ordinary light vibrate in all different planes). The polarized light beams in DIC microscopes refract at different degrees by the different parts of a thin, transparent, and unstained specimen, are collected by a prism, and then quantified. The image generated is sharp and appears three-dimensional (Fig. 2.3). The specimen needs to be thin and transparent t be examined by a DIC scope.
Fluorescence microscope

For fluorescence microscopy, the specimens are stained with a fluorochrome. A fluorochrome is a chemical substance that emits light when excited by a light beam. A fluorescent microscope is a compound microscope equipped with an appropriate light source to excite the fluorochromes of the fluorochrome-stained specimen. The image of the specimen appears to glow on a dark background (Fig. 2.4).
Fig. 2.4. Fluorescence and confocal microscopy. A. Optics of a fluorescent microscope. A light beam of wavelength

494 nm is projected onto a specimen labeled with fluorescein (a fluorochrome). The labeled specimen absorbs light energy and then emits green light at a wavelength of 521 nm. B. Legionella pneumophila, a bacterium stained with fluorescein-labeled antibodies, appears to glow on a black background when examined by a fluorescence microscope. Image courtesy: CDC-PHIL. C. Optics of a confocal microscope. A laser beam excites fluorochromes of the fluorochrome-labeled specimen. The excitation light and the emitted light rays are scanned, accurately focused, and finally recorded by a detector. D. A confocal image of Bacillus anthracis, a bacterium. The cell wall appears green and the endospores of the bacterium appear red. Image courtesy: CDC-PHIL.
Confocal microscopes

A confocal microscope examines a fluorochrome-stained specimen after exciting the fluorochrome with a laser beam. The specimen can be fixed before fluorescent staining, or unfixed live cells can be fluorescently stained and examined. A set of mirrors or acoustic optical deflectors scans both the excitation light and the light emitted by the fluorochrome-stained specimen. Scanning is conducted across the specimen by moving the mirrors and tilting the specimen stage. The emitted light is then focused on a pinhole and collected by a detector. A computer program assembles the image by adding the images of consecutive sections of the specimen (Fig. 2.4). The overall image is crisp and can be rendered three-dimensionally.

blocks.text: An electron microscope is like a vacuum tube that produces an electron beam from a cathode (the negative electrode). The electron beam is then used to image or scan a specimen. Since the wavelength of the electron beam is very short (0.004-0.012 nm, compared to about 500 nm for visible light), the resolving power of electron microscopes (EMs) is much superior to LMs. There are various types of EMs, and transmission electron microscopes (TEMs) and scanning electron microscopes (SEMs) are the most commonly used.

In a TEM, a metallic electromagnetic condenser lens focuses an electron beam onto a specimen (Fig. 2.5). The specimen is fixed, embedded in epoxy plastic, thinly sliced, and then placed on a copper grid. The specimen is stained with a heavy-metal salt, such as uranyl acetate or lead acetate. Different structures within the specimen absorb the heavy metal ions at different concentrations. When electrons pass through the specimen, some are scattered by the heavy metal ions. The electron beam that passes through the specimen carries the information of the specimen. The beam is magnified by electromagnetic objective lenses and projected onto a fluorescent viewing screen. As a result, a visible image of the specimen develops that can be seen by the naked eye or recorded by a sensor to generate a computer-generated image (Fig. 2.5). A simple TEM can magnify up to 100,000x and resolve at 2.0 nm. A highly sophisticated TEM may magnify up to fifty million-fold and resolve at 0.05 nm. Cellular elements such as membranes and organelles can be clearly viewed with a TEM. Fixing and staining the samples can introduce artifacts in TEM images.
Fig. 2.5. Electron microscopy. A. Structure of a TEM (left) and an SEM (right). Important components of the

microscopes are shown. The focused electron beam is shown in pink. Redrawn after figures of SEM and TEM designed by JEOL USA Inc, Peabody, MA. B. A TEM image of a part of a human cell (magnified ~50,000x). The nucleus, lipid membranes, mitochondria, ribosomes, and type C retrovirus particles present in the cell are indicated. Image courtesy: CDC-PHIL. C. An SEM image of Hartmannella vermiformes, an amoeba (magnified ~2,500x), showing the surface details of the organism. Image courtesy: CDC-PHIL.

An SEM uses a focused electron beam to scan the specimen (Fig. 2.5). The specimen's exposed surface is coated with carbon, tungsten, or gold nanoparticles. As the electrons hit the coated specimen, they lose some energy. The lost energy generates heat, light, or gamma radiation and low-energy secondary electrons. A sensor detects one of the above (usually the secondary electrons) and feeds the information to a computer. A computer program then generates a composite black-and-white image of the specimen's surface contour. An SEM can only image the surface details of the specimen. SEMs may magnify up to 10,000x and resolve up to 20 nm (Fig. 2.5). Both SEM and TEM generate only black-and-white images, but these images can be converted to false-color images using computer programs.

blocks.text: The structure of an idealized bacterium is shown in Fig. 2.6. Not all bacterial species possess all the features shown in the figure. The features are described in the following sections, beginning with the external features.
Fig. 2.6. Schematic of an idealized bacterial cell. Shown are the basal body with a flagellum, capsule, cell wall,

cytoplasm, inclusion bodies, nucleoid, pili, plasma membrane, plasmid DNA, and ribosomes (not drawn to scale). Flagellum Flagellum (pl. flagella) is a whip-like structure. A flagellum has three major parts: a basal body made of 2-5 discs embedded in the membrane, a whip-like filament (5-20 nm in length) made of a globular protein named flagellin), and a hook that attaches the basal body to the filament (Fig. 2.7). The basal body serves as a molecular motor. The motor rotates at a rate of 200-1,000 rotations/sec if protons pass through the basal body. When the motor rotates counterclockwise, the bacterium moves forward (run). When the motor rotates clockwise, the cell tumbles without forward motion.
Fig. 2.7. Bacterial flagella and motility. A. The basal body of a flagellum. Various protein components of the basal

body and their attachment to the plasma membrane and the cell wall of a Gram-negative bacterium are shown. Redrawn after Xing J, Berry R, Oster G. PNAS 2006, 103(5): 1260-1265. B. Distribution of flagella on bacterial cells. Monotrichous- one flagella at one pole, lophotrichous- a tuft of flagella at one pole, peritrichous- many flagella over the cell surface, amphitrichous- a tuft of flagella at each pole of the cell, sheathed- flagella under the external membrane. A cross-section of a spirochete is shown to illustrate the location of the sheathed flagella. C. A simplified illustration of bacterial motility. When the basal body rotates counterclockwise, the bacterium moves forward (run); when the basal body rotates clockwise, the bacterium tumbles with no forward movement.

Depending on the species, a bacterial cell may lack flagella or have one or a few flagella. Flagella are generally exposed to the outer surface, but some bacteria (spirochetes) have internal or sheathed flagella (under the membrane). Bacteria with external flagella achieve motility through repeated run and tumble, in a zigzag fashion, while bacteria with sheathed flagella move like a corkscrew. Motility, also known as taxis, allows the cell to avoid unpleasant or harmful environmental conditions (such as extreme temperature, pH, and the presence of dissolved toxic chemical substances), and move toward a nutrient-rich, pleasant environment. In a uniform environment, motile bacteria move randomly. Bacteria that normally live in aquatic environments usually have flagella, but they may stop producing flagella when grown under drier conditions. Many pathogenic (disease-causing) bacteria have flagella. Thus, the flagellum can be a virulence factor (a factor that helps pathogens cause infection more efficiently). Pilus A pilus (plural pili) is an external hair-like growth (1-20 nm in length) on the cells of some bacterial species. The filament of the pilus is made of many copies of a globular protein named pilin (Fig. 2.8). Additional proteins anchor the pilus to the plasma membrane. There are several types of pili. Fimbriae are shorter, thinner pili that help bacteria attach to surrounding surfaces. There could be an adhesive disc at the tip of the fimbriae. The type IV pilus allows a bacterium to anchor itself on a surface and then move towards the surface by shortening the length of the pilus. Bacterial nanowires are modified pili used by some bacteria to transport electrons. A sex pilus of a bacterium transports DNA to another bacterium by a process known as conjugation (see Chapter 6). Many pathogenic bacteria generate pili.
Fig. 2.8. Pili of bacteria. A. Cells of the bacterium Salmonella enteritidis with many flagella and fimbriae (indicated

thick and thin arrows, respectively). Courtesy: CDC-PHIL/James Archer. B. Finer structure of a type IV pilus of a Gram-negative bacterium. The pilus is mostly made of many units of PilA proteins, but other proteins such as PilQ and PilC help the pilus attach to the cell. Redrawn after Bakkali M. Arch Microbiol 2013; 195(4): 279-89. C. Two bacteria (Rickettsia felis) connected by a sex pilus in the process of conjugation. The bacterium on the bottom appears to have some fimbriae. Image source: Ogata H, Renesto P, Audic S, et al. PPLOS 2005; https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0030248.
Glycocalyces

Some bacterial species secrete a glycocalyx (a mass of polysaccharide and or polypeptide molecules) into their surroundings. It is called a capsule if the secreted materials remain firmly attached to the bacterial cell (Fig. 2.9) or slime if the secreted materials are only loosely attached to the bacterial cell. If many bacterial cells share the same mass of glycocalyx, the structure is called a biofilm (Fig. 2.9). Glycocalyx prevents bacteria from desiccation and also from harmful chemicals from touching bacterial cells. Organisms that eat bacteria find it difficult to catch bacteria surrounded by the slippery glycocalyx. Biofilm can grow in human tissues and more readily on inanimate objects inside the human body, such as intrauterine devices, catheters, pacemakers, and implants. Biofilm may also occur in the environment. An extensive bacterial biofilm grown on a plastic surface is used to treat municipal wastewater.
Fig. 2.9. Bacterial biofilm. Shown is a TEM image of Staphylococcus aureus cells growing on the lumen of a catheter.

Many bacteria (white balls) are present in this network of capsular materials. Image courtesy: CDC-PHIL. Cell wall With a few exceptions, all bacterial species contain a cell wall. The cell wall gives shape to the bacterial cell and helps it withstand osmotic pressure (the pressure on the plasma membrane due to water from the surrounding environment entering the cytoplasm). The bacterial cell wall is composed of peptidoglycan (also called murein), found only in bacteria. Peptidoglycan has a polypeptide (hence peptido-) and polysaccharides (hence -glycan) components. The polysaccharide is made of two modified hexose sugars, N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM). The NAM entity is linked to a short polypeptide made of four to five amino acids (Fig. 2.10). The polypeptide chains of two different neighboring polysaccharide chains are cross-linked by a third polypeptide chain (Fig. 2.10) to provide strength to the cell wall.
Fig. 2.10. Bacterial cell wall. A. Structure and location of the cell wall. A. The glycan. A glycan chain is made of

about 100 NAG-NAM repeats. The NAM entity has a short polypeptide chain. Image courtesy: Roujeinikova A. PNAS 2008; 105(30) 10348-10353. B. Peptides of peptidoglycan. The NAM entities of two different polysaccharide molecules are cross-linked by a third ‘cross-linking’ polypeptide. C. The locations of the cell wall relative to the plasma membrane in G(+) bacteria, G(-) bacteria, and some actinobacteria. 1- plasma membrane, 2- peptidoglycan cell wall, 3- lipoteichoic acid (LTA) outcrop; 4- outer membrane, 5- lipopolysaccharide (LPS) layer, 6- arabinogalactan cell wall, 7- mycolic acid outcrop.

Bacteria are grouped into four different categories based on the location of the cell wall relative to the plasma membrane of the cell (Fig. 2.10). In Gram-positive (G+) bacteria, a thick peptidoglycan cell wall forms the outer shell of the cell, and the cell wall is traversed by many molecules of lipoteichoic acid (LTE). LTE are made of lipid and polysaccharide components. In Gram-negative (G-) bacteria, a thin peptidoglycan cell wall lies between two different lipid membranes. Actinobacteria (a type of G+ bacteria), have an external arabinogalactan cell wall outside the peptidoglycan cell wall to which long lipid chains (mycolic acids) could be attached. A few known bacterial species (of Family Mycoplasmacea) lack a cell wall, but they have two membranes as in G(-) bacteria. The plasma membranes The plasma membrane surrounds the cell's watery cytoplasm. The plasma membrane is made of phospholipids, glycolipids, and some proteins (Fig. 2.11). Some bacteria have hopanoids (ring-shaped organic compounds), but all bacteria lack cholesterol, which is found in the plasma membrane of all eukaryotes. The lipid molecules are arranged in two layers and serve as a barrier to the free passage of molecules across the membrane. The membrane proteins could be on the outer face, the inner face, or across the lipid bilayer. The proteins reinforce the lipid layer and serve as receptors and transport channels. Since the lipid and protein molecules of the membrane stay together by weak forces (not tied together by covalent bonds), the membrane is called a fluid mosaic. The fluid mosaic changes shape if pushed, but does not break into pieces like solid or liquid substances.
Fig. 2.11. A schematic of the bacterial membranes. The lipid molecules are shown by the blue balls and lines, and

the proteins are indicated as pink ellipses and cylinders. The cell wall above the plasma membrane shows the polysaccharide chains made of NAG and NMA (squares). The left third of the figure is for actinobacteria, the middle third is for G(+) bacteria, and the right third is for G(-) bacteria. Note the locations of mycolic acid, LTA and LPS relative to the plasma membrane and cell wall. Redrawn after Barry CE, Crick DC, McNeil MR. Infect Disord Drug Targets 2016; 7(2): 182-222. Abbreviations: 1- the outer leaf of the outer membrane (mostly LPS), 2- porins, 3- inner leaf of the outer membrane, 4- periplasmic space, 5- plasma membrane, 6- membrane proteins, 7- Galactofuran chains, 8- Arabinofuran chains, 9- mycolic acid chains.

The G(-) bacterial cells have an outer membrane (envelope) outside the cell wall (Fig. 2.11). The envelope is also made of two lipid layers. The inner layer of the envelope structurally resembles the plasma membrane, but the outer layer is dominated by an unusual molecule called lipopolysaccharide (LPS). LPS is made of lipid and polysaccharide components. The space between the outer shell and the plasma membrane of a bacterial cell is the periplasmic space. Peptidoglycan (PG), LTA, LPs, and mycolic acid (Fig. 2.12) are part of the cell and are released only by dead bacteria. Once released, these molecules, especially LPS, bind to membrane receptors and activate the leucocytes. Leucocytes then secrete powerful mediators such as cytokines. As a result, the host animal develops various disease signs, including fever. These molecules (PG, LPS, and LTA) are also known as bacterial endotoxins. LTA and LPS, pili and glycocalyces, allow bacterial cells to adhere to other cells and inanimate surfaces. Thus, these molecules are also known as adhesins. Note that pathogenic bacteria also secrete exotoxins. Unlike endotoxins, exotoxins are proteins and only live bacterial cells secrete them (see Chapter 10).
Fig. 2.12. LTA, LPS, and mycolic acid. The fatty acid components of the molecules are indicated by the zigzagged

lines (i.e., the skeletal structure). A. LTA, found in the cell wall of some G(+) bacteria. B. LPS, found in the outer layer of the outer membrane of all G(-) bacteria. C. Mycolic acid molecules are linked to the arabinogalactan layers of the cell wall of some actinobacteria (especially mycobacteria).
Cytoplasm and its components

Protoplasm refers to all components of the cell combined, whereas cytoplasm includes everything inside the plasma membrane. Cytoplasmic contents include cytosol, inclusion bodies (insoluble particles), and organelles (i.e., tiny organs). The cytosol is mostly water (about 80% by volume) and dissolved molecules such as RNA, proteins, sugars, amino acids, and various ions. The local concentrations of the dissolved or suspended molecules vary greatly. The cytoplasm may exhibit liquid, semisolid (gel), and nearly solid (glass-like) phases.
Inclusion bodies

Different bacterial species contain different types of inclusion bodies. Inclusion bodies include stored food substances such as glycogen granules, fat droplets, phosphate granules (also called metachromatic or volutin particles), sulfur particles, and iron beads (also called magnetosomes) (Fig. 2.13). Aquatic bacteria may also have protein-coated gas bubbles for buoyancy.

Endoplasmic membrane and membrane-bound organelles Bacteria generally lack endoplasmic membranes and membrane-bound organelles. Some photosynthetic bacteria, such as Chlorobium sp., contain membrane-bound organelles called chlorosomes (Fig. 2.13).
Ribosomes

Ribosomes are the most abundant particles in the cytoplasm. Bacterial ribosomes are about 20 nm in diameter and are made of 65% RNA and 35% protein. Ribosomes are essential for protein synthesis. Bacterial ribosomes exist as small (the 30S) and large (the 50S) subunits. The 30S and 50S subunits form 70S particles when they are engaged in protein synthesis (Fig. 2.13). Here, the letter S stands for Svedberg unit, related to the sedimentation of the particles (one S unit is 1x10-13 seconds).
Fig. 2.13. Some inclusion bodies and organelles are found in bacterial cells. A. Yellow sulfur particles in a sulfur

bacterium of the genus Beggiatoa. Image- Wikipedia. B. A magnetosome in the iron bacterium Magnetospirillum magnetotacticum (TEM image, the bar is 1 μM, Image-IGEM.org). C. Chlorosomes of the green bacterium Chlorobium tepidum. Image from Frigaard N, Voigt GD, and Bryant DA. J Bacteriol 2002; 184:3368-3376). D. Bacterial 30S and 70S ribosomes.
The nucleoid

The nucleoid occupies the central region of the cytosol (Fig. 2.14). The cell's genome stays here, and RNAs are synthesized here. Bacterial genomes consist of one or more dsDNA molecules, which can be linear or circular. Cells’ genomic DNA molecules are called chromosomes because they are always bound to some proteins. A bacterial genome can have 0.5-10 million base-pairs of nucleotides, and the size varies between 0.2-3.5 mm. Since the nucleoid is about 0.001 mm in diameter, the chromosome is meticulously folded to fit inside the nucleoid. In addition to chromosomes, some bacteria contain plasmid DNA in the nucleoid.
Fig. 2.14. Bacterial nucleoid and genome. A. A TEM image showing the bacterial nucleoid present in the center of

the cell. Image source: CDC-PHIL. B. A TEM image showing chromosomal DNA oozing out of a damaged bacterial cell. The bacterium was treated with lysozyme, an enzyme that destroys the bacterial cell wall. The images were magnified by about 30,000x. Image source: www.colorado.edu.
Bacterial spores and endospores

Some species of the bacterial genera Actinomyces, Streptomyces, and Micromonospora produce spores as a means of reproduction. These soil bacteria appear as filaments; spores form at the tips of the filaments (Fig. 2.15). The spores disperse as they are detached from the bacterial filament. The spores germinate when they fall into a suitable growth environment, producing new bacterial filaments. Some bacteria, such as Chlamydia trachomatis, cannot survive outside the host cells. These bacteria produce spore-like particles that may survive outside the host cell for a short time before infecting another host cell. The bacterial spores described above can be easily destroyed by boiling or using common antibacterial chemical agents.
Fig. 2.15. Bacterial spores and endospores. A. Spores of Streptomyces sp. A photomicrograph showing spores at

the end of the bacterial cell. The spores are about 1.5 micrometers in diameter. Image source: CDC-PHIL. B. Spores (called elementary bodies) of Chlamydia trachomatis. Shown is a TEM image of a dead cell. The spores are about 0.2 micrometers in diameter. Image source: http://microwiki.kneyon.edu. C. Endospores (and vegetative cells) of Clostridium perfringens. Shown is a phase-contrast image of a spread of an old bacterial culture (courtesy Prof. MR Sarker, Oregon State University).

Some genera of soil bacteria, such as Bacillus and Clostridium, produce spores that can withstand high temperatures and many chemical disinfectants (Fig. 2.15). These spores are called endospores because they remain inside the walls of the mother cells until the mother cell is degraded. One bacterial cell produces one endospore when exposed to harsh environmental conditions, such as desiccation and nutrient deprivation. These bacteria produce endospores to overcome inclement environmental conditions. The endospores germinate when conditions are favorable, producing a vegetative bacterium. Note that vegetative bacteria absorb nutrients and divide, but spores and endospores do not; they remain dormant until they germinate. Endospores of some pathogenic bacteria, such as Bacillus anthracis and Clostridium tetani, may germinate on the body surfaces and cause disease.

sections.heading: Morphology and clustering of bacterial cells

blocks.text: Bacterial species may differ in cell size and shape (i.e. morphology). When cells of some bacterial species divide, the daughter cells may stay attached to their parent cells and divide again, forming cell clusters. Bacterial species grown on semisolid media produce colonies of specific shapes, sizes, and colors. Bacterial cell morphology, cell clustering, and colony morphology can be helpful in identifying a bacterial species.
Bacterial cell morphology

Bacterial cells can be roughly divided into five different morphological forms: coccus (plural- cocci), bacillus (plural- bacilli), coccobacillus (plural- coccobacilli), branched filamentous, and pleomorphic. A coccus is spherical or ovoid in shape (Fig. 2.16). A bacillus is a straight or a curved rod. A straight bacillus can be fusiform, with a thicker midsection and tapered ends. A curved bacillus with only one curvature is a vibrioid cell, and a bacillus with two or more curvatures is a spirillar cell (Fig. 2.16). A curved bacillus is called a spirochete if the cell is very thin (diameter about 0.09 micrometer) and long (3-30 micrometers) and with several curvatures along the longitudinal axis (Fig. 2.16). Spirochetes are so thin that they cannot be visualized by an LM unless stained by a fluorescent dye. A coccobacillus is elliptical in shape where the length is only slightly bigger than the breadth of the cell. One may confuse a coccobacillus with a coccus or a short bacillus.

Filamentous bacteria produce a long thread-like growth called hyphae, which can be branched. Cells of a particular bacterial species growing in a particular environment appear nearly identical in shape and size. However, bacteria lacking a cell wall can have any given shape. In some bacterial species, cells may appear different in size and shape. Such species are called pleomorphic bacteria (Fig. 2.16).
Fig. 2.16. Morphological structures of bacterial cells and bacterial clustering. A. Diagrams of a coccus, a

coccobacillus, and various types of bacilli are shown. Bacteria lacking a shape and bacteria that develop hyphae are also shown. B. Clustering of bacterial cells. A diplococcus contains two cocci; a tetrad contains four cocci, a sarcina contains eight cocci; a streptococcus is a linear chain of many cocci; a staphylococcus group is like a cluster of grapes; and a steptobacillus forms a linear or a branched filament of multiple cells. C. Typical and pleomorphic bacteria. Clustering of bacterial cells When bacterial cells divide, the daughter cells may stay together and form bacterial clusters. Thus, a coccus may divide and produce a diplococcus (two cells in a cluster), a tetrad (four cells in a cluster), or a sarcina (eight cells in a cluster). Such clusters (Fig. 2.16) may break during further cell division. Some species of cocci divide only in one plane and form a long chain of cells, forming a structure called streptococcus (Fig.2.16). Some cocci may divide in all possible planes and produce a cluster of cells like a bunch of grapes, a structure called staphylococcus (pl. staphylococci, Fig. 3.16). Bacilli usually divide only at the long axis. Some species of bacilli form a linear cluster called streptobacillus (pl. streptobacilli, Fig 3.16), and some form branched filaments called hyphae (Fig. 2.16). Note that three bacterial genera, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and Streptobacillus, are named so because of the clustering of the cells. However, cells of the other bacterial genera may show similar clustering abilities. For example, the cells of some species of the genus Enterococcus may cluster as streptococci or staphylococci.

The eukaryotic cell described below is an idealized one (Fig. 2.17). A typical eukaryotic cell is spherical with a diameter of about 10-25 μm. The volume of an average eukaryotic cell is about ~8,000 μm3 and that of a bacterial cell is about 4 μm3. Thus, an average eukaryotic cell is about 2,000-fold larger (by volume) than a bacterial cell. Here is a description of various structures of a eukaryotic cell, from the outside toward the center. The description is brief, mainly to contrast with the structure of bacterial cells.
Flagella, cilia, kinetosome, and centrioles

A eukaryotic cell may contain one (as in mammalian spermatozoa) or a few flagella (as in Giardia lamblia, a protozoan), or many cilia (as in the lung epithelial cells and Paramecium aurelia, a protozoan). Cilia (sing. cilium) are the shorter flagella. Bacterial and eukaryotic flagella are functionally related (both aid motility), but structurally unrelated.

A eukaryotic flagellum is thicker and longer than bacterial flagella (diameter 0.5 micrometers, length up to 10 micrometers) and is covered by the plasma membrane. The flagellum is composed of ten pairs of microtubule fibers (nine fused pairs encircling an un-fused central pair) forming a structure called an axoneme (Fig. 2.17). The eukaryotic flagellum is a complex structure made of some 250 different polypeptides. Only a summary of the structure of the eukaryotic flagella is presented here.

Eukaryotic flagella (Fig. 2.17) are attached to the cells through a structure called the basal body or kinetosome. The kinetosome originates from a centriole. The cell usually possesses two centrioles, but they may produce daughter centrioles to generate flagella. The centrioles are also made of microtubules. The centrioles are also necessary for the production of spindle fibers required for cell division.
Fig. 2.17. The eukaryotic cell and flagellum. A. Structure of a eukaryotic cell, showing some of the components.

Image- Human Genome Research Institute. B. Eukaryotic flagellum. The flagellum is covered by the plasma membrane. Note the 9 pairs + 2 microtubule arrangement in the axoneme and the 9 triplets of microtubules arrangement at the kinetosome. The diameter of a flagellum is about 0.5 micrometers, and a flagellum can be about 15 micrometers in length. Image source: https://bio.libretexts.org/.

Eukaryotic flagella move (undulate due to the movement of the tubulin fibers) like a whip. The dynein and kinesin proteins of the microtubule motors hydrolyze ATP, which provides the energy for flagellar undulation. Some cells (such as spermatozoa) use flagella for movement. Tissue-bound cells, such as flagellated epithelial cells on the mucous membranes, use flagella to remove foreign particles that may otherwise settle on the cell surface. Some eukaryotic flagella function as a sensory organelle.
Cell wall

The cells of plants, algae, and fungi contain a cell wall (Fig. 2.18). The cell wall of plant and algal cells is made of cellulose and other polysaccharides, such as amylose, pectin, and amylopectin. The cell wall of fungi contains polysaccharides such as chitin, glucan, and mannan, as well as some glycoproteins. Some animal cells may contain cell walls made of calcium salts (as in eggshells) or silicates (in some protozoa).
Fig. 2.18. The cell wall of some eukaryotic organisms. A. Plant cell wall showing polysaccharide fibers

(hemicellulose, pectin, and cellulose microfibrils) over the plasma membrane. The middle lamella (made of calcium and magnesium pectate) stays between neighboring cells in plant tissues. Image source: https://openi.nlm.nih.gov/. B. The fungal cell wall (schematics). The components of the cell wall may change at different stages of the life cycle of a fungus. Image source: Geohegan I, Steinberg G, Gurr S. Trends Microbiol 2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.tim.2017.05.015. The cell walls of multicellular eukaryotes are perforated to allow communication between neighboring cells. As in bacteria, the cell wall in eukaryotes gives rigidity and helps the cell withstand osmotic pressure. The plasma membrane and the endomembrane system The plasma membrane of eukaryotic cells is structurally similar to that of prokaryotic cells, except that it also contains cholesterol. Eukaryotic cells contain a large volume of internal membrane, called the endoplasmic reticulum, and many membrane-bound organelles, including the Golgi apparatus, various types of membrane vesicles, the nucleus, mitochondria, and chloroplasts (described later in this section).

The purpose of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is to increase the internal surface area of the cell (Fig. 2.19). Proteins are synthesized in the rough ER where many ribosomes are anchored to the ER. Lipids and many other molecules are synthesized and processed in the smooth ER. The synthesized molecules are then translocated to other parts of the cell or to the exterior via various membrane vesicles derived from the ER, including endosomes and lysosomes. Lysosomes contain various hydrolytic enzymes. Plant cells have a large vesicle called the central vacuole in the middle region of the cell for storing nutrients and waste. Endosomes, which can also form at the plasma membrane, bring external molecules into the cell. The movement of molecules via transport vesicles from the cell to the outside is exocytosis, and from outside to inside is endocytosis. The membrane vesicles may fuse with other endosomes or membranes of some membrane-bound organelles (see Chapter 9).
Fig. 2.19 Dynamic nature of the endomembrane system. Generation, movement, and fusion of the membrane

vesicles are shown schematically. The blue, red, and green arrows indicate membrane trafficking, endocytosis, and exocytosis, respectively. SER- smooth endoplasmic reticulum; RER- rough endoplasmic reticulum. Not shown in the figure are the COP I, COP II, and clathrin proteins that help pinch the vesicles of the plasma membrane, the Golgi Complex or ER, and the receptor-ligand system that helps the vesicles fuse to another membrane. The cytoskeleton Although bacteria have a cytoskeleton, it is more prominent in eukaryotic cells. Cytoskeleton is a dynamic network of protein fibers that can be grouped into three categories: microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments (Fig. 2.20).

Microtubules (hollow tubes made of alpha and beta tubulin, 25 nm in diameter) are involved in the movement of cells (by flagella and cilia) and the movement of membrane vesicles and organelles inside the cell. During cell division, microtubules move the sister chromatids or homologous chromosomes to the daughter cells.

Microfilaments, the polymers of the proteins alpha- and beta-actin, help move cytoplasm and smaller molecules. The microfilaments are about 7 nm in diameter, but several of them may work together. Microfilaments are assembled and disassembled rapidly.

The polymers of intermediate filaments are about 10 nm in diameter (thus smaller than microtubules but larger than microfilaments) and made of diverse protein units such as keratin, lamin, neurofilament, and vimentin (depending on the cell type). The crisscrossing of the intermediate filaments provides the cell with structural strength. Intermediate filaments and microfilaments mostly determine a cell's overall shape.
Fig. 2.20. The dynamic cytoskeleton. The cytoskeleton of a live endothelial cell is shown on the top. The actin

filaments are stained red, the microtubules are stained green, and the nucleus is stained blue. Image from NIH Image- Program packet. The line drawings of the tubulin, microfilament, and intermediate filaments are from unknown artists (from the Creative Commons).

Adjacent cells in a tissue of metazoan animals are attached to each other through cytoskeletal proteins, forming various types of junctions, including tight junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions (Fig. 2.21). The cells of a tissue may also be anchored to fibers in the basement membrane (the basal lamina) via structures such as hemidesmosomes (Fig. 2.21). Enzymes secreted by some microbes may degrade protein fibers and damage tissue structure.
Fig. 2.21. Cell-to-cell and cell-to-basement membrane attachments. A tight junction seals the membranes of the

adjacent cells by transmembrane proteins such as claudins and occludins. The adherens junctions join the microfilament bundles of the adjacent cells. The desmosomes connect intermediate filament bundles of the adjacent cells. The gap junctions allow cell-to-cell passage of water-soluble ions through transmembrane channels made of connexons. Finally, the hemidesmosomes attach cells to the basal lamina (the basal lamina contains various fibers including laminin, collagen, perlecan, and entactin).
Cytosol

Due to the presence of extensive ER and cytoskeletal proteins, the cytosol (the liquid portion of the cytoplasm) of the eukaryotic cell is highly compartmentalized. As in bacteria, the eukaryotic cytoplasm contains both soluble and insoluble components, including naked organelles. In addition, eukaryotic cells have many membrane-bound organelles.
Naked organelles

Naked organelles lack a membrane cover. Naked organelles include the centrioles and the ribosomes. Centrioles are paired organelles, each containing nine triplets of microtubules (Fig. 2.22). The ribosomes of eukaryotic cells are structurally similar to bacterial ribosomes (Fig. 2.13) but larger. The small (40S) and the large (60S) ribosome particles of eukaryotic cells join to form 80S particles. Many of the 80S ribosome particles are engaged in protein synthesis while attached to the ER and constitute the rough ER.
Fig. 2.22. The centrioles and the Golgi apparatus. A. Centrioles are paired organelles, each containing nine triplets

of microtubules. Microtubules radiate from the centriole to produce structures such as spindle fibers and flagella. Image from Creative Commons. B. A Golgi apparatus. Shown is a TEM image of the Golgi complex of a leukocyte. The series of lamellae and the surrounding transport vesicles are visible. The longest lamella of the Golgi apparatus in a mammalian cell is about one micrometer in length. Image source: Wikipedia.
The Golgi apparatus

Golgi apparatus, named after Camillo Golgi (1843-1926), is a dynamic set of apposed membrane lamellae (Fig. 2.22). A cell can have multiple Golgi apparatuses. Proteins and lipids synthesized in the ER are transported to the Golgi complex via transport vesicles. Enzymes in the Golgi complex modify lipids, process and modify proteins, and transport the processed molecules to different destinations via transport vesicles.
The nucleus

The nucleus is one of the largest organelles in the eukaryotic cell. Most cells have a single nucleus, but some have two or more. In general, the nucleus is a circular organelle located in the center of the cell. Two concentric bilayer membranes, called the nuclear envelope, surround the nucleus. The envelope is dotted with many pores called nuclear pores (Fig. 2.23). The nucleus houses the chromosomes. DNA replication, RNA transcription, and RNA processing occur in the nucleus. The location of the nucleus where ribosomal RNAs are synthesized forms a structure called the nucleolus.

The eukaryotic cells contain two or more linear dsDNA chromosomes. The chromosomes of a resting (i.e., non- dividing) cell is organized as chromatin. Note that bacterial chromosomes do not form the chromatin structure, although archaeal chromosomes do form a structure similar to chromatin. Chromatin is formed because of the binding of chromosomal DNA to a type of protein called histones. Chromatin fibers found inside the nucleus are 11-30 nm in thickness, and the fibers are dispersed in the nucleus. During cell division (mitosis and meiosis), the nuclear envelope breaks down, and chromatin condenses into thicker fibers, ultimately forming butterfly-shaped mitotic chromosomes (Fig. 2.23). The mitotic chromosomes are composed of two sister chromatids tied by a protein known as cohesin.
Fig. 2.23. The nucleus and the chromosome. A. The nucleus showing the nuclear membrane, nuclear pores, nuclear

channels, and a nucleolus. B. The nuclear genome. The 2.0 nm wide dsDNA spools around balls made of histone proteins to make 11 nm chromatin fibers. The 11 nm chromatin fibers further fold to produce 30 nm chromatin fibers. These chromatin fibers further fold to form the thick mitotic chromosomes (1,400 nm in thickness) during cell division. Image: Du H, et al. Science 2017; 357:6 .349. DOI: 10.1126/science.aag0025.
Mitochondria

Nearly all eukaryotic cells (except a few groups of protozoa) contain numerous mitochondria (Fig. 2.24). Mitochondria (sing. mitochondrion) are endosymbiotic bacteria. Like bacteria, mitochondria contain circular double-stranded DNA chromosomes and (smaller) ribosome particles, and mitochondria divide like bacterial cells. However, unlike typical bacteria, mitochondria contain an extensive endoplasmic membrane. Mitochondria synthesize ATP for the cell, metabolize toxic substances, and influence host cell death by a process called apoptosis.
Fig 2.24. The common endosymbionts of the eukaryotic cells. A. Structure of a mitochondrion (schematic) showing

the outer membrane, the inner membranes or the cristae, and the matrix. B. A schematic of a chloroplast showing the outer membrane and the inner membrane structures such as the thylakoids and grana and the stroma. Figures from Creative Commons.
Chloroplasts

Chloroplasts are found in plant and algal cells and a few protozoan cells (Fig. 2.24). Like mitochondria, chloroplasts are bacterial cells; they have their own chromosomes, ribosomes, and endoplasmic membrane. Chloroplasts have various pigments, including chlorophylls, which absorb light energy and allow chloroplasts to generate ATP. The excess ATPs that chloroplasts synthesize are used to synthesize food energy molecules, such as glucose and polysaccharides.
The endosymbiosis theory

Two organisms living together are symbionts, and the process is symbiosis. An endosymbiont lives inside the cell of its symbiotic host. Endosymbiosis is considered a major driving force of the evolution of eukaryotic cells and the modern-day mitochondria and chloroplasts. The Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowsky (1855-1921) proposed the theory in 1905. Lynn Margulis (b. 1938) extended the scope of the theory in the 1960s. The premises of the widely accepted version of the theory are shown in Fig. 2.25.

The theory suggests that the ancestral eukaryotic cells lacked a nucleus. The cell evolved and became larger, necessitating the development of endoplasmic membranes. Ultimately, the nucleoid of the ancestral cell got surrounded by a nuclear envelope. The newly evolved eukaryotic cell was anaerobic (survived without oxygen). An aerobic bacterium invaded the ancestral eukaryotic cell and, in time, evolved to the present-day mitochondria. Since mitochondria synthesize abundant ATP, the symbiotic relationship benefited the eukaryotic cell. Some of these eukaryotic cells later engulfed photosynthetic bacterial cells. Those photosynthetic bacterial cells evolved into chloroplasts. The host eukaryotic cells offer nutrients and many other amenities to the endosymbionts. As a result, the bacterial partners have lost many genes and large portions of their genomes, becoming completely dependent on host eukaryotic cells for shelter.
Fig. 2.25. The endosymbiosis theory. The three premises of the theory are elaborated in the figure. Figure courtesy:
Phil Schatz/ Wikimedia.

Endosymbiosis is common in nature. A good example is the bacterial genus Wolbachia and its eukaryotic partners, such as the worm Wuchereria bancrofti. In this symbiosis, the bacterial partner provides key nutrients (such as vitamins and coenzymes) essential for the survival or success of the host organisms, and the eukaryotic partner provides shelter and some nutrients. In the process, the bacterial partner has lost some of its genes, while the host cells have become dependent on it. If Wuchereria bancrofti is treated with antibiotics such as tetracycline (which kill Wolbachia but not eukaryotic organisms), the endosymbionts would be eliminated, thereby inhibiting the growth of Wuchereria bancrofti or even killing it.

blocks.text: Live cells can be examined without staining using a contrast-enhancing microscope. However, for a more detailed examination, cells are processed, stained, and then examined.
Fixing

Cells (and tissues) are initially fixed to keep the structure of cellular molecules and organelles intact during processing and staining. Cells with a cell wall (bacteria, algae, and fungi) can be fixed by placing the cells on a glass slide in a small amount of water, allowing the water to evaporate, and then briefly passing the slide over a flame. Animal cells and tissues, being fragile, need more elaborate fixing. Formalin (formaldehyde solution), or glutaraldehyde, organic chemicals that crosslink proteins, is used to fix animal cells.
Processing

Fixed cells and tissue slices are dehydrated and then embedded in wax (for LM) or epoxy plastic (for TEM). The embedded tissue is then thinly sliced using a microtome (a mechanical device that uses a blade). The thin slices are placed on a glass slide (for LM) or copper grid (for TEM), set there by warming, and then stained. For SEM, the fixed cells or tissues are coated with carbon (graphite) or metal (e.g., tungsten) nanoparticles using specialized coating devices.

slides.title: Staining for LM examination
bullets: Other processing steps for animal cells and tissues
Attaching and staining on a slide

blocks.text: Stains include dyes and pigments (for LM), and heavy-metal salts (for TEM). Unlike dyes and metal salts, pigments are insoluble in water. Dyes and pigments (Table 2.2) appear colored because they contain certain chemical components called chromophores.
Table 2.2. Common dyes and pigments used for staining.

Type of dye Color Major applications Basic dyes Carbol fuschin Red Acid-fast staining (bacteria) Crystal violet Deep violet Gram staining (bacteria) Hematoxylin Red Staining tissue slices (eukaryotes) Malachite green Bluish-green Endospore staining Methylene blue Blue Counterstaining/simple staining of bacteria Safranin Red Counterstaining and simple staining of bacteria Toluidine blue Blue Staining tissue slices (eukaryotes) Metal salts Uranyl acetate Lead acetate No color Staining samples for TEM imaging Acidic dyes Eosin Red Simple staining of bacteria or leucocytes Nigrosin Black Staining spermatozoa (mixed with eosin) Neutral dyes India ink (soot) Black Negative staining, capsule staining Giemsa (methylene blue and eosin) Violet Staining leucocytes Fluorescent dyes DAPI Glows blue Staining DNA in the nucleus Fluorescein Glows green Antibody-bound dye used in staining Rhodamine Glows red Antibody-bound dye used in staining Chromospheres absorb certain wavelengths of visible light and reflect light of other wavelengths. The wavelengths reflected by the dyes determine their color. Thus, a chromosphere that absorbs all visible wavelengths (i.e., violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, and orange) but reflects red light (wavelength ~700 nm) appears red to the viewer. However, fluorescent dyes emit light (i.e., glow) when they absorb light of certain wavelengths (Fig. 2.26). For example, fluorescein (a fluorescent dye) absorbs light of wavelength 494 nm (cyan) and emits green light at 512 nm (Fig 2.26).

When a dye (or a salt) dissolves in water, they dissociate into cations and anions. If the (positively charged) cation holds the chromophore, it is a basic dye; if the (negatively charged) anion holds the chromophore, it is an acidic dye. The cell is negatively charged due to the presence of many phosphate groups (-PO4) in nucleic acids and membrane lipids. Thus, the basic dyes bind to cells via electrostatic interactions. Acidic dyes and pigments do not bind to the cell; instead, they are deposited on the background, making the sample appear in perspective.

The metal cations in the metal salts also bind the negatively charged entities in the cell. Many fluorescent dyes do not bind cellular molecules. Those fluorescent dyes are attached to an antibody, which then binds to a protein of the cell.

sections.heading: Staining bacterial cells for LM examination

blocks.text: Simple staining

A drop of a bacterial culture is placed on a slide. When water evaporates, the slide is warmed over a flame, which fixes and attaches the cells on the slide. A bacterial smear is then covered with a basic dye, such as safranin, for a minute. The dye is then rinsed off, and the slide is examined under a LM. The cells appear pink (if safranin is used) on a white background (Fig. 2.27).
Fig. 2.26. How staining works. A. A stain XA dissolved and dissociated in water to X+ and A-, and the X+ component

is the fluorochrome. It binds to some negatively charged components of the cell. When illuminated by white light (i.e., the mixture of all seven visible light, violet, indigo, blue, green, orange, yellow, and red), the chromophore absorbed all wavelengths but reflected the red light. The stained sample appeared red to the observer. B. How fluorescent staining works. Fluorescent dyes are usually inert. They are attached to an antibody that binds to the cell. When the antibody-tagged fluorescein dye-stained cells are exposed to cyan light (wavelength 494), the dye absorbs the light and emits green light (wavelength 512 nm). The sample appears green to the observer.
Negative staining

Negative staining uses dyes or pigments that do not stain but reveal the outline of cells or their exudates, such as the capsule. Negative stains may not stain the background (as acidic stains do). Nigrosin and India ink are the common pigments used for negative staining. A small sample of bacteria is mixed with a suspension of the pigments and then thinly smeared on a glass slide. The slide is air-dried and then examined under an LM; cells or cellular structures, such as capsules, appear white (or semi-transparent) against a dark background (Fig. 2.27).
Fig. 2.27. Stained bacteria examined using an LM. A. Simple staining- The bacterium Serratia marcescens stained

with safranin. Image courtesy: Ken Slater, Utah Valley University. B. Negative staining/capsule staining of Bacillus anthracis using India ink. Image source: CDC-PHIL. C. Gram staining of a mixture of G(-) cocci and G(+) cocci and bacilli. The G(+) bacilli and cocci appear dark purple, the (G(-) cocci appear light pink. Image courtesy: Ken Slater, Utah Valley University. Magnification of all specimens was about 1,000x.
Differential staining
Differential staining uses a multistep procedure to distinguish bacterial species or growth stages within a species. Some of the common differential staining methods are described below.
Gram staining

This method was originally developed by the Danish microbiologist Hans Christian Gram (1853-1938) in 1884. Gram staining helps differentiate G(+) and G(-) bacteria. For Gram staining, a thin smear of bacteria fixed on a glass slide is briefly (about a minute) soaked with crystal violet dye. The stain is washed away with water, and the smear is covered with an iodine solution for about one minute. Iodine serves as a mordant, an agent that helps some structures of the cell retain the crystal violet dye. Iodine is then washed off with water, and the slide is briefly de-stained with ethyl alcohol or an alcohol-acetone solution. At this point, bacteria with a thick cell wall, such as G(+) bacteria, retain some of the crystal violet dye; however, the G(-) bacteria with a very thin cell wall lose all the crustal violet dye. The slide is then rinsed with water, and the smear is counterstained with another basic dye, such as safranin or methylene blue, for about one minute. The counterstain is then removed by briefly washing with water. When the stained slide is examined with a LM, the G(+) cells appear dark purple, and the G(-) cells appear pink (if safranin is used as the counterstain) (Fig. 2.27).
Ziehl-Neelsen (or acid-fast) staining

Some actinobacteria, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, are difficult to stain with common stains because of the waxy mycolic acid layer on the cell surface. These bacteria require special staining methods such as acid-fast staining. In acid-fast staining, the bacterial smear on a glass slide is covered with a paper towel soaked with a solution of carbol fuschin (a mixture of phenol and fuschin), and the slide is heated over a flame for 3-5 minutes so that the dye may penetrate through the waxy coat of the bacterium. The slide is then cooled and de-stained using an acid- alcohol solution (usually 0.5-5.0% hydrochloric acid in ethanol).

The acid-alcohol solution dissolves and removes the red dye from ordinary bacterial cells, but the acid-fast cells retain the dye. The slide is then washed with water and counterstained with methylene blue for one minute. The slide is then briefly washed with water, and then excess water is removed from the slide by a paper towel. When examined using an LM, acid-fast cells appear dark red because the cells do not absorb the methylene blue dye. Non-acid-fast bacteria, if present, appear blue (Fig. 2.28). The Ziehl-Neelsen method can also be used in staining endospores.
Fig. 2.28. Some differential staining processes. A. Acid-fast staining. Sputum of a patient stained by the acid-fast

technique. The presence of red bacilli indicates the presence of acid-fast bacteria in the person's sputum. B. Endospore staining. A smear of endospore-forming Bacillus stained with malachite green and counter-stained with safranin. The endospores are stained deep green. C. Flagella stain. Bacillus coagulans stained with Leifson flagella stain. All the images are magnified ~1,000x. All three images are from CDC-PHIL.
Schaeffer-Fulton endospore staining

A thin smear of spore-forming bacteria is fixed on a glass slide and then covered with a paper towel soaked with malachite green dye. The slide is heated over a flame for five minutes. The slide is then cooled to room temperature, rinsed with water, and then counterstained with safranin. When the slide is examined under a bright-field LM, the cells appear red and the endospores green (Fig. 2.28). Bacterial endospores can be visualized without staining by examining spore-forming bacteria using a phase-contrast microscope (Fig. 2.15). The endospores appear as points of light because they are highly dehydrated and thus more refractile.
Leifson flagella staining

Bacterial flagella may not be visible if the cells are heat-fixed (because the heat may destroy flagella). In addition, nutrients in the bacterial culture media may adhere to flagella, making them difficult to stain. For flagella staining, the cells are washed in distilled water to remove any nutrient particles and then placed on a warm glass slide. The smear is air-dried for 15 minutes, and then a drop of Leifson stain (a mixture of tannic acid, pararosaniline, sodium chloride, and ethanol) is placed on the slide. The slide is left at room temperature until it is almost dry. The slide is examined immediately under a bright-field LM. The bacteria and flagella appear reddish (Fig. 2.28) because of the deposition of pararosaniline (a red organic basic dye) and tannic acid on the cells.

sections.heading: Staining eukaryotic microbes for LM examination

blocks.text: Eukaryotic cells are quite large and can be examined by an LM with minimal preparation and staining. The LM, however, reveals only the outline and some minor details of the interior of the eukaryotic cells. Algae Most algae have pigments (because they have chloroplasts), so staining is unnecessary for examining algal cells. A wet mount (a small amount of a cell suspension on a glass slide under a coverslip) can be examined directly under an LM. Algal cells and their chloroplasts are visible at relatively low magnification (Fig. 2.29). Fungi Fungi in saliva or vaginal secretions can be smeared on a glass slide in a small drop of water. The slide is air-dried and then stained with iodine solution or calcofluor white stain containing 10% potassium hydroxide. The latter method is preferred because potassium hydroxide dissolves contaminating human cells. Calcofluor is a fluorescent dye that binds cellulose and chitin. The slide is examined under a UV-capable microscope. Fungal skin infections can be examined directly by scraping the skin onto a glass slide and then staining it with calcofluor white before examination (Fig. 2.29).

Mold can also be examined by wet mounting. A small sample of mold growing on bread or a rotting fruit is transferred to a glass slide using a pair of forceps. A smear is made by adding a few drops of mounting medium (water, 1% lacto- fuschin dye, or 1% lactophenol cotton blue dye). The smear is covered with a coverslip and examined under an LM. The stained mold and spores appear pink (if lacto-fuschin is used), or blue (if lactophenol cotton blue is used) for staining.
Fig. 2.29. Microscopic examination of algae and fungi. A. A simple wet mount of Spirogyra sp., a freshwater alga

(x400). The ribbon-like chloroplast and the cell walls are clearly visible. Image from Wikipedia. B. Malassezia globosa, a skin fungus treated with calcofluor white in 10% potassium hydroxide (x1,000). Image from http://www.scielo.org.ar/. C. Lacto-phenol cotton blue-stained Aspergillus fumigatus, a fungus (x400). Spore-bearing aerial hyphae and many spores are shown. Image- CDC-PHIL.
Protozoa

A smear of protozoan parasites is made on a glass slide, fixed by evaporating the fluid, and then stained with iodine, Wright-Giemsa, eosin, or hematoxylin-eosin stain. The stain is removed, and a cover slip is placed on the stained sample before examination under a LM (Fig. 2.30). Giardia lamblia and its cysts can be examined in concentrated fecal samples after staining with hematoxylin (Fig. 2.30).
Worm eggs and cysts

Worm eggs in fecal samples can also be examined under LMs. The fecal sample is diluted in normal saline (0.9% NaCl) and filtered through cheesecloth to remove undigested food debris. The filtrate is centrifuged at 500xg for 5-10 minutes. The supernatant is removed, and the pellet is suspended in a 10% formalin solution to fix the microbes. The fixing solution is mixed with 0.4 volume of ethyl acetate (to improve sedimentation of the microbes). The mixture is centrifuged again at 500xg for 5-10 minutes, and the supernatant is removed. The pellet is suspended in a 10% formalin solution. A drop of this solution is then placed on a glass slide, stained with iodine, Wright-Giemsa, eosin, hematoxylin-eosin, or trichrome stain, and examined under an LM (Fig. 2.30).
Fig. 2.30. Microscopic examination of protozoan parasites and worm eggs. A. Trichomonas vaginalis, a protozoan

parasite that infects genitourinary tracts, stained with Giemsa stain (x1,00). B. Giardia lamblia, a protozoan parasite of the intestinal tract, stained with the trichrome stain, (x1,000). C. An egg of the nematode worm Ascaris lumbricoides stained with hematoxylin, (x1,000). D. A larva of Trichinella sp. in the tongue muscle of a rat. The tissue section was stained with hematoxylin-eosin stain. The original image was magnified 400x. The larva is in a pathologically extended single muscle cell. Images A, B, and C from CDC-PHIL; image D from CDC-DPDx.
